gloss: Three core metrics for recruitment cost
verbatim: The true cost of recruitment is typically measured through three interlocking metrics: cost-per-hire (CPH), time-to-fill, and cost-of-vacancy (COV), each capturing a different dimension of what an open position actually costs an organization.

gloss: CPH is the most standardized metric
verbatim: Cost-per-hire is the most standardized of the three.

gloss: CPH formula codified in 2012 by SHRM/ANSI
verbatim: The formula was formally codified in 2012 through a joint effort between the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI)[1].

gloss: SHRM/ANSI definition of CPH
verbatim: The SHRM/ANSI standard defines CPH as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires"[1]

gloss: CPH cost components: internal vs external
verbatim: encompassing both internal costs (recruiter time, internal systems) and external costs (agency fees, job board postings, advertising) incurred to fill open positions[1]

gloss: LinkedIn's CPH definition
verbatim: LinkedIn's recruiting metrics guide offers a consistent definition: total spend associated with filling an open position (recruiter fees, advertisements, etc.) divided by the number of hires[1].

gloss: Definitions vary in emphasis despite shared formula
verbatim: Despite this shared underlying formula, different organizations and publications phrase the definition with varying emphasis on which cost components to include[1].

gloss: Time-to-fill vs time-to-hire often conflated
verbatim: Time-to-fill and time-to-hire are related but distinct time-based indicators that are frequently conflated.

gloss: Time-to-fill definition
verbatim: Time-to-fill measures the number of days between when a job requisition is opened or approved and when a candidate accepts the offer (in some organizations, when the new hire starts)[2][3]

gloss: What time-to-fill reflects
verbatim: and reflects the overall efficiency of the hiring process as well as the organization's competitiveness for talent[3]

gloss: Time-to-hire definition
verbatim: Time-to-hire, by contrast, measures the days between a candidate entering the pipeline and offer acceptance[2]

gloss: Time-to-hire is a narrower window than time-to-fill
verbatim: a narrower window focused on pipeline efficiency rather than the full requisition-to-offer cycle.

gloss: 2024 time-to-fill benchmark: 54 days
verbatim: The 2024 benchmark for time-to-fill is approximately 54 days[2].

gloss: Cost-of-vacancy definition
verbatim: Cost-of-vacancy (COV) quantifies the cost of leaving a position unfilled

gloss: COV factors depend on position, industry, lifecycle stage
verbatim: and the underlying factors that determine it are largely dependent on the position, the industry, and the current stage of the product lifecycle[4].

gloss: Average revenue per lost employee calculation
verbatim: **Average revenue per lost employee**: a company's total revenue divided by its number of employees, then divided by the number of working days in a year (220), yielding the average daily revenue an employee generates — revenue that is not produced while the position sits vacant[4].

gloss: Salary multiplier of revenue lost calculation
verbatim: **Salary multiplier of revenue lost**: a calculation based on the premise of lost revenue relative to the position's salary[4].

gloss: Advice to build COV formula with finance department
verbatim: Organizations building a COV formula are advised to develop it in conjunction with the finance department

gloss: Why involve finance early on COV
verbatim: since finance's early involvement adds credibility to the calculations and preempts resistance to the resulting figures[4].

gloss: Levers exist to reduce recruitment time and cost
verbatim: Several levers are commonly cited as reducing both the time and cost dimensions of recruitment:

gloss: Employee referrals as a lever
verbatim: encouraging internal employee referrals, which are a cost-effective sourcing channel and tend to produce higher-quality hires who align with company culture[5]

gloss: Optimizing job descriptions as a lever
verbatim: optimizing job descriptions to attract genuinely qualified candidates and reduce time spent sorting irrelevant resumes[5]

gloss: Pre-employment assessments as a lever
verbatim: using pre-employment assessments to gauge candidate skills and fit, reducing the risk of a bad hire[5]

gloss: Automating recruitment tasks as a lever
verbatim: automating repetitive recruitment tasks such as resume screening, interview scheduling, and follow-up messaging[2]

gloss: Maintaining a warm talent pipeline as a lever
verbatim: maintaining an active, warm talent pipeline through talent communities and proactive sourcing rather than starting to source only after a requisition is approved[2]

gloss: Definition of cost of vacancy (COV)
verbatim: Cost of vacancy (COV) is the metric used to quantify the actual business impact of a talent shortage created by the gap between when a role is needed and when the recruiting function can fill it[4].

gloss: What COV can be configured to measure
verbatim: It can be configured to measure the dollar impact of voluntary and involuntary turnover, or the impact of a recruiting process too slow to meet an organization's growing talent needs[4].

gloss: COV has no standardized formula, unlike CPH
verbatim: Unlike cost-per-hire, there is no magic or standardized formula for calculating cost of vacancy, because the factors involved vary by role and organization[4].

gloss: Simplified estimation used except for key roles
verbatim: Many organizations therefore use a simplified estimation formula rather than calculating the true, fully-loaded cost for every position, reserving detailed calculation for key roles[4].

gloss: COV range $7k-$12k/day, up to $200k/day for time-to-market critical roles
verbatim: In roles where time-to-market is a critical driver of corporate success, the cost of a single vacancy has been calculated at between $7,000 and $12,000 per day, and in one documented case reached as high as $200,000 per day[4].

gloss: Simplified $100/day vacancy-productivity-loss estimate
verbatim: One source ties a simplified vacancy-productivity-loss estimate to roughly $100 per day the role remains unfilled[6]

gloss: Example: 45-day open sales role costs $112,500 in lost revenue
verbatim: illustrates the scale effect with a senior sales role left open for 45 days costing an estimated $112,500 in lost revenue[7].

gloss: CPH is the most standardized recruitment-cost metric
verbatim: Cost-per-hire is the most formally standardized recruitment-cost metric.

gloss: CPH codified in 2012 by SHRM/ANSI
verbatim: It was codified in 2012 through a joint effort between the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), which defines CPH as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires"[1].

gloss: The Cost Per Hire formula
verbatim: Cost Per Hire = (Total Internal Costs + Total External Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires[1][8][7]

gloss: SHRM Human Capital Benchmarking's CPH definition
verbatim: SHRM's Human Capital Benchmarking describes CPH as the total of all internal and external, direct and indirect costs associated with sourcing, recruiting, and staffing an open position, divided by number of hires[1].

gloss: HCI's CPH definition
verbatim: The Human Capital Institute (HCI) defines it as all recruitment advertising, agency, travel and interview, relocation, referral bonus, and recruiter compensation/benefits costs divided by total new hires in the period[1].

gloss: CIPD's CPH definition
verbatim: The UK's CIPD defines cost per hire as the average cost of filling a vacancy, including internal labor (recruitment staff and pro-rated interviewer time) plus external costs (job adverts, agency fees), divided by number of hires[1].

gloss: LinkedIn's CPH definition
verbatim: LinkedIn's recruiting metrics guide similarly defines CPH as total spend on filling an open position (recruiter fees, advertisements, etc.) divided by number of hires[1].

gloss: CPH formula is consistent but implementation varies
verbatim: While the fundamental formula is consistent across these sources, implementation is not: some organizations exclude indirect costs like hiring managers' time for simplicity, while others include onboarding costs even though this is not standard practice

gloss: Recommendation to document CPH methodology for comparability
verbatim: making it important for organizations to document their exact CPH methodology so comparisons stay apples-to-apples[1].

gloss: Internal CPH cost components
verbatim: Internal cost components typically include recruiting staff salaries and benefits (fully loaded cost of in-house recruiters and talent acquisition team members), prorated salaries of HR staff or hiring managers for interviewing/recruiting time, recruiting department overhead (office infrastructure, equipment, compliance costs), and internal sourcing costs such as employee referral bonuses[1][8].

gloss: External CPH cost components
verbatim: External costs include job board fees, agency fees, advertising, background checks, drug testing, skills assessments, and candidate travel expenses[8][6].

gloss: Direct vs indirect cost split, indirect is 60-70% of true total
verbatim: One source separates these into "direct costs" (job advertising, agency fees, background checks, assessments — the costs most commonly tracked) versus "indirect costs," which it estimates make up 60–70% of the true total and include manager/team interview time, productivity loss during the vacancy period, administrative processing, onboarding and training, equipment/software setup, and the productivity gap during new-hire ramp-up[6].

gloss: 2026 guide: teams undercount CPH by omitting hidden costs
verbatim: A 2026 guide notes that most teams still undercount CPH because they omit manager time leakage, tool-stack bloat, no-show interviews, and the productivity hit of an unfilled seat

gloss: Example: $3,000 vs $10,000+ per hire gap explained by inputs not formula
verbatim: explaining why two companies hiring similar roles can report $3,000 vs. $10,000+ per hire, since it is the inputs rather than the formula that explain the gap[9].

gloss: Worked example: $8,000 CPH from $400,000/50 hires
verbatim: A company that spent $300,000 on internal costs and $100,000 on external costs to hire 50 people has a cost per hire of $8,000 ($400,000 ÷ 50)[8].

gloss: Worked example: $6,000 CPH from $60,000/10 hires
verbatim: A business spending $60,000 on hiring activities in one quarter while bringing on 10 new employees has a cost per hire of $6,000 ($60,000 ÷ 10)[10].

gloss: Worked example: $4,700 CPH from 5 October hires
verbatim: Five hires made in October with $7,000 in internal costs and $16,500 in external costs yields $4,700 per hire (($7,000 + $16,500) ÷ 5)[11].

gloss: Worked example: $1,875 CPH from 40-person company, 8 roles
verbatim: A 40-person company filling 8 roles in a quarter with $6,000 in external costs (job board posts, background checks, one contingency agency fee) and $9,000 in internal costs (hiring manager and recruiter time) yields $1,875 per hire (($6,000 + $9,000) ÷ 8)[9].

gloss: Recommended practice: quarterly cadence for gathering cost data
verbatim: gather cost data from finance reports and HR systems for a chosen time period (quarterly is described as the most practical cadence — enough volume for a useful number without waiting too long to spot a trend)

gloss: Recommended practice: cross-reference totals against accounting records
verbatim: cross-reference totals against accounting records for accuracy

gloss: Recommended practice: count whole hires, not fractional FTEs
verbatim: count whole hires rather than fractional full-time-equivalents

gloss: Recommended practice: avoid mismatched cost/hire periods
verbatim: avoid comparing costs and hires from mismatched periods (e.g., annual costs against monthly hires)[8][9]

gloss: CPH benchmarks vary by source/year/scope
verbatim: Reported average CPH figures vary by source and year, reflecting differing scope and survey timing.

gloss: SHRM cross-industry CPH average ~$4,700
verbatim: SHRM's cross-industry average is commonly cited at approximately $4,700[10].

gloss: Percentile breakdown of CPH
verbatim: One source's percentile breakdown gives a 25th percentile of $500, a median of $1,633, a 75th percentile of $4,669, and an average of $4,425[11]

gloss: Median US CPH ~$1,633, executive CPH up to $28,000
verbatim: another cites a median U.S. cost per hire of approximately $1,633 alongside executive-level hires reaching upwards of $28,000[12].

gloss: 2026 guide: updated SHRM 2025 CPH average $5,475/$35,879, 21% increase since 2022
verbatim: A 2026 guide states the $4,700 average is now outdated, citing SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report as putting the real U.S. average at $5,475 for non-executive roles and $35,879 for executive roles — a 21% increase from 2022[9].

gloss: Another source's CPH figures: $4,683 non-executive, $28,329 executive
verbatim: Another source gives $4,683 for non-executive roles and $28,329 for executive roles[7].

gloss: Time-to-fill and time-to-hire are distinct, not interchangeable
verbatim: Time-to-fill and time-to-hire are related but distinct efficiency metrics, and sources caution against using them interchangeably[13][14].

gloss: Definition of time-to-hire
verbatim: Time-to-hire is defined as the time from when a candidate applies to when they accept an offer, and is a candidate-centered indicator of process speed within the selection stages (screening, interviewing, accepting offers)[13][14].

gloss: Definition of time-to-fill
verbatim: Time-to-fill begins earlier — at job requisition approval or posting — and runs through offer acceptance, encompassing the entire recruitment timeline including job approval and posting, making it the longer of the two measures[13][14][2].

gloss: Time-to-fill formula
verbatim: The formula for time to fill is: Time to Fill = Date candidate accepts offer − Date job requisition was approved or opened;

gloss: Worked example: 24-day time to fill
verbatim: a requisition opened March 1 with an offer accepted March 25 yields a time to fill of 24 days[2].

gloss: 2024 benchmark: average time to fill ~54 days
verbatim: One 2024 benchmark cites an average time to fill of approximately 54 days[2].

gloss: Time-to-fill vs time-to-hire diagnose different delay sources
verbatim: Both metrics are described as within an organization's control and useful for diagnosing where delays occur: time-to-fill reveals delays before candidates apply (approvals, job description clarity, recruiter bandwidth), while time-to-hire reveals delays after candidates enter the pipeline (interviews, assessments, offer negotiation)[2].

gloss: Recommendation to track both metrics as a diagnostic pairing
verbatim: Tracking only one metric gives an incomplete picture — time to fill alone doesn't capture candidate experience, and time to hire alone misses broader organizational bottlenecks — so sources recommend monitoring both together as a "diagnostic pairing"[2].

gloss: Fully loaded employee cost reaches 1.25x-2.5x base salary
verbatim: Separate from recruitment-specific cost metrics, the fully loaded cost of employing one person — including base salary, payroll taxes, health insurance contributions, retirement matching, workers' compensation, equipment, software licenses, and workspace — is estimated to routinely reach 1.25 to 2.5 times base salary[7].

gloss: Itemized true-cost example for a $50,000 salary hire
verbatim: For a $50,000 annual salary hire, the itemized estimate is: base salary $50,000; employer payroll taxes (FICA, FUTA, SUTA) approximately $4,500; health insurance employer contribution $6,000–$8,000; workers' compensation $500–$1,500; equipment $1,500–$3,000; software licenses/tools $500–$2,000; onboarding and training time cost $2,000–$4,000; for a total estimated first-year cost of $65,000–$74,000, or 1.3x to 1.48x base salary (reaching 2x or higher for roles with specialized equipment, higher benefits, or significant training needs)[7].

gloss: Definition of direct/external costs
verbatim: Direct costs — also referred to as external costs, since they represent money paid outward to third-party vendors rather than absorbed internally — are the most straightforward and quantifiable component of cost-per-hire (CPH), covering expenses that can be pointed to on a receipt and attached to one hire and one recruitment cycle[15].

gloss: SHRM average CPH benchmark and its caveat
verbatim: Benchmarks vary by source: SHRM places the average U.S. cost per hire at roughly $4,700 to $5,475, though this figure captures mostly direct costs and doesn't reveal whether it's good or bad without accounting for role mix, company size, and industry[15][16].

gloss: Wider CPH range by role level, escalating with time-to-fill
verbatim: Other industry research puts cost-per-hire in a wider range of $4,000–$20,000 depending on role level, with costs escalating the longer a position remains open[17].

gloss: CPH scope boundary excludes post-hire costs
verbatim: Notably, cost-per-hire is bounded at getting an employee to day one — it excludes post-hire costs like training beyond onboarding, productivity ramp-up, or ongoing employment costs, which belong to separate metrics like cost-of-vacancy and time-to-productivity[16][8].

gloss: Job board/sourcing costs are a foundational direct expense
verbatim: Job board and sourcing costs form a foundational direct expense.

gloss: Job posting fee ranges (general, Indeed minimum, LinkedIn per-click)
verbatim: Job posting fees run roughly $50–$500 per posting[18], though a single posting on Indeed has a minimum of around $150, and LinkedIn ads can charge roughly $5–9 per click[19].

gloss: Monthly job ad spend in competitive/global hiring markets
verbatim: In competitive markets, monthly job ad spend across multiple boards can run $500–$2,000 or more for a single role, and multinational firms hiring globally may spend more by localizing job boards or running social media campaigns in each region[19].

gloss: Additional advertising cost categories (social media, print, careers page)
verbatim: Costs also include social media advertising, print media, and career/careers page maintenance and updates (mobile optimization, current design)[20][21].

gloss: Advertising cost pattern by role level
verbatim: By role level: entry-level roles typically rely on broad job board postings and university career sites (lower cost); mid-level roles may need more targeted ads or professional network promotion; executive searches often skip public ads altogether, relying instead on specialized recruiters whose fee covers much of the "finding" work[19].

gloss: Agency fees are one of the largest direct/external line items
verbatim: Agency and third-party recruiter fees are consistently cited as one of the largest direct/external line items[19][18].

gloss: Contingency search fee structure and rate range
verbatim: **Contingency search** (common for mid-level roles): typically 15%–25% of the hire's first-year salary[15][19][8][18], with some niche or executive searches reaching up to 30%[19].

gloss: Contingency search worked fee example
verbatim: Example: a $70,000-salary role could carry a $10,500–$17,500 agency fee[19].

gloss: Contingency search trade-off: volume over quality vetting
verbatim: Contingency firms are paid only on placement, and because multiple firms often compete for the same placement, this model can favor volume over quality, with less thorough vetting and reduced access to passive candidates[22].

gloss: Retained search fee structure and rate range
verbatim: **Retained search** (standard for C-suite and senior executive roles): 25%–35% of total first-year compensation (base salary plus projected bonus)[19][22], sometimes reaching up to 40% for retained search generally[18], and up to 40%–50% of first-year income for C-level roles (CEO, CFO, CTO) at the top end[22].

gloss: Retained search fee paid in three installments
verbatim: Fees are typically paid in three installments: roughly one-third upon engagement, one-third when qualified candidates are presented, and the balance on placement[22].

gloss: Retained search minimum and senior-executive fee amounts
verbatim: Some firms set minimum fees between $80,000 and $100,000 depending on the position's salary, with fees for senior executives readily exceeding $150,000[22].

gloss: Hybrid/retingency/container fee model
verbatim: **Hybrid/"retingency"/container models**: a lesser upfront fee of 10%–25% of the total, with the remainder paid on placement — a middle ground best suited to director- and VP-level searches[22].

gloss: Additional executive-search costs beyond the base fee
verbatim: **Additional executive-search costs**: administrative fees of 10%–15%, plus travel, background checks, assessments, and marketing costs that can add another 5%–15% to the total engagement price[19][22].

gloss: Agency fee comparison across role levels with dollar examples
verbatim: By role level, entry-level hires carry the smallest absolute fees even at higher percentages (e.g., 20% of a $30,000 salary = $6,000), mid-level roles are "very often" filled via agencies at the 15%–25% rate, and executive hires can dwarf all other hiring costs — a 30% fee on a $200,000 executive salary equals $60,000[19].

gloss: Geographic and industry variation in agency fees
verbatim: Geographic and industry variation is significant: agencies in major metros (New York, San Francisco, Chicago) and in talent-scarce sectors (technology, financial, health sciences) command premium fees; in the UK, agencies commonly charge ~20% for general roles, but specialized searches can exceed £19,000 in fees[19][22].

gloss: Background check cost ranges (basic vs comprehensive)
verbatim: Basic background checks (criminal history, identity verification) run $30–$50[6], or $20–$50 per candidate in another estimate[19], while comprehensive packages (credit history, education/degree verification, employment history) cost $100–$150[6] to $100–$200[19].

gloss: Drug testing cost range
verbatim: Drug testing adds $30–$110 depending on the panel and whether it's lab-based[6].

gloss: Screening costs multiply across the whole candidate pipeline, not just the hire
verbatim: These costs multiply across every candidate screened in a pipeline for one role, not just the eventual hire[19].

gloss: Pre-employment skills assessment cost range
verbatim: Pre-employment skills assessments and testing tools cost $30 to $200 per candidate screened[16].

gloss: Screening/assessment cost pattern by role level
verbatim: By role level, entry-level hiring may involve more candidates and thus more (but cheaper per-candidate) checks; mid-level hires may use specialized assessments such as management aptitude tests that cost more per use; executive hiring involves the most extensive and priciest vetting (detailed background investigations, executive assessment services) despite a smaller candidate pool[19].

gloss: Employee referral bonus range
verbatim: Employee referral bonuses range from $500 to $5,000 per successful hire[16].

gloss: Candidate travel/lodging/meal costs count toward CPH
verbatim: Candidate travel and lodging expenses for out-of-town onsite interviews, along with meal stipends, count toward cost-per-hire[21].

gloss: Relocation assistance cost range and delivery method
verbatim: Relocation assistance, when applicable, can add $5,000 to $20,000+ per hire[16], delivered either as a lump sum after acceptance or as direct payment for moving, lodging, and travel costs, varying by seniority level[21].

gloss: Career fair and event participation costs
verbatim: Direct/external costs also include job fair and career-event participation: booth or presence fees, marketing materials (brochures, banners, promotional items), and recruiter travel, lodging, and meals for attending events[20][21].

gloss: Employer branding spend and amortization treatment
verbatim: Employer branding and sponsored content spend tied to recruiting is another external category[10][9], and when included, careers page and employer branding spend should be prorated annually and amortized across total hires[16].

gloss: Recruitment technology/software cost and per-hire allocation
verbatim: Recruitment technology and software — applicant tracking systems (ATS), video interview platforms, assessment tools — often carry subscription or licensing fees that factor into CPH, generally spread across all hires as HR overhead and amounting to a few hundred dollars per hire on average, though this adds up especially for smaller companies investing in enterprise-grade tools[23][19][21].

gloss: Other miscellaneous external costs: legal fees and exit costs
verbatim: Other cited external/miscellaneous items include legal fees for drafting employment contracts, and exit costs (severance, benefits continuation) when a hire is a replacement[20].

gloss: Worked example of a small company's blended cost-per-hire calculation
verbatim: One illustrative calculation: a 40-person company filling 8 roles in a quarter incurred $6,000 in external costs (job board posts, a couple of background checks, and one contingency agency fee) and $9,000 in internal costs (hiring manager and recruiter time), for a combined $15,000 ÷ 8 hires = $1,875 per hire — well below the SHRM average, which is expected given the company isn't filling executive or specialized technical roles at enterprise volume[9].

gloss: Definition of indirect/soft costs as the largest, non-invoiced share of hiring cost
verbatim: Indirect costs, often called soft costs, are the expenses of recruitment that never appear on an invoice yet typically make up the largest share of what a hire actually costs an organization[15].

gloss: Indirect costs are harder to measure than direct costs
verbatim: Unlike direct costs, which are easy to itemize, indirect costs are tied to time, productivity, and risk, and are therefore harder to measure and easy to underestimate[15].

gloss: Indirect costs estimated at 60-70% of total hiring cost
verbatim: Industry estimates place indirect costs at roughly 60-70% of the true total cost of hiring[6],

gloss: Indirect costs estimated at 3-10x direct costs for a bad hire
verbatim: while other analyses put them at 3-10 times larger than direct costs specifically in the context of a bad hire[24].

gloss: SHRM's $5,475 cost-per-hire figure only captures direct costs; real total 2-3x higher
verbatim: SHRM's widely cited average cost-per-hire figure of about $5,475 (elsewhere cited as roughly $4,700-$5,475) captures mostly direct costs; once indirect costs are added, the real total often runs two to three times higher[15].

gloss: Internal staff time spent on hiring tasks is a major indirect cost source
verbatim: A substantial share of indirect cost comes from the hours internal staff spend on the hiring process rather than revenue-generating work: writing job descriptions, reviewing resumes, conducting interviews, and scoring candidates[15][19].

gloss: In-house TA specialist salary works out to ~$2,000 per hire
verbatim: If an in-house Talent Acquisition specialist earns $60,000-$80,000 per year and handles approximately 40 hires annually, that works out to roughly $2,000 per hire in salary cost alone, before counting the time of hiring managers and interview panel members[19].

gloss: Extra interview rounds multiply time cost across panel members
verbatim: Each additional interview round multiplies this further, since panels typically involve two or more managers or team members whose time must also be costed in[19].

gloss: Small businesses without HR see indirect costs exceed direct costs
verbatim: For small businesses without a dedicated HR function, this burden falls disproportionately on the founder or manager, whose time is often the most expensive resource in the company; as a result, indirect costs for small businesses typically exceed direct costs[25].

gloss: Unfilled roles carry a direct productivity cost
verbatim: Unfilled roles carry a direct productivity cost.

gloss: SHRM 2020 study: monthly cost of a vacant position
verbatim: A 2020 SHRM study found the average cost of a vacant position ranges from $4,129 to $5,733 per month, depending on industry and role, and can run significantly higher for high-demand positions in technology or healthcare[26].

gloss: Vacancy productivity loss estimate of ~$100/day
verbatim: One estimate puts vacancy productivity loss at roughly $100 per day a role sits open[6].

gloss: Average time to fill has risen from 29 to 43 days since 2010
verbatim: Compounding this, the average time to fill a U.S. position has risen to 43 days, up from 29 days in 2010, according to LinkUp[26] — meaning the vacancy-cost window has grown substantially over the past decade.

gloss: Vacancy period effects: overtime burden, morale, productivity, lost customers
verbatim: During this period, existing employees often absorb the missing workload through overtime, and organizations can face decreased morale, reduced productivity, and even lost clients or customers due to diminished service levels[26][15].

gloss: Onboarding indirect costs after offer acceptance
verbatim: Once a candidate accepts an offer, indirect costs continue through onboarding: HR and manager time spent on orientation, onboarding software or materials, and sometimes travel, lodging, or a welcome package for the new hire[19].

gloss: Average U.S. onboarding cost benchmark
verbatim: Benchmarks put average U.S. onboarding cost at roughly $1,500-$5,000 per employee[19].

gloss: Training has both direct and indirect (lost productivity) costs
verbatim: Training carries both direct costs (course fees, trainer salaries, e-learning subscriptions) and indirect costs, since a new hire in training is not yet fully productive[23][19].

gloss: Productivity gap persists through ramp-up period
verbatim: This productivity gap persists through the ramp-up period, as the new employee builds toward full effectiveness[6][15].

gloss: Administrative processing costs tied to each new hire
verbatim: Indirect costs also include administrative processing tied to each new hire: payroll setup, benefits enrollment, equipment provisioning, and records work[15][27].

gloss: Employee benefits should be factored into hiring-cost assessment
verbatim: Employee benefits associated with new hires — health insurance, retirement contributions, and other perks — vary by the organization's compensation structure but should be factored into any comprehensive hiring-cost assessment[23].

gloss: A mis-hire is the most expensive indirect cost
verbatim: The most expensive indirect cost is a mis-hire.

gloss: Gallup: replacing an employee costs 50-200% of annual salary
verbatim: Gallup estimates that replacing an employee costs 50% to 200% of their annual salary[6][15][25].

gloss: Concrete replacement cost examples for entry-level vs senior roles
verbatim: Applied concretely: a $50,000 entry-level position carries roughly $25,000 in replacement costs, while a $100,000 senior role can run $200,000 or more[6].

gloss: Replacement cost figures include rehiring plus vacancy/ramp-up productivity losses
verbatim: These figures capture the full cost of rehiring plus productivity losses during the vacancy and the ramp-up of the replacement[6].

gloss: Bad-hire indirect costs beyond replacement search, 3-10x direct costs
verbatim: Beyond the replacement search itself, a bad hire generates indirect costs including lost leadership time, team productivity drag, missed performance targets, delayed projects, and negative cultural impact — costs that are typically 3-10 times larger than the direct costs of hiring[24].

gloss: Decision guidance: when cost of waiting on a struggling hire exceeds restarting the search
verbatim: Decision guidance on this point: if role clarity and performance expectations were clear from the start and a performance gap persists after 60-90 days of focused support, the cost of continuing to wait on a struggling hire typically exceeds the cost of restarting the search[24].

gloss: Organizations tracking only invoiced spend miss the larger indirect-cost half
verbatim: Because hard costs are visible on a ledger and soft costs are diffused across many people's time, organizations that track only invoiced spending are managing the smaller half of their hiring budget while flying blind on the larger half[15].

gloss: Comprehensive cost-per-hire formula sums external and internal costs
verbatim: The comprehensive cost-per-hire formula accounts for this by summing both categories: Total Cost-Per-Hire = (External Costs + Internal Costs) ÷ Number of Hires[27],

gloss: Components that make up internal costs in the formula
verbatim: with internal costs comprising internal HR time, hiring manager time, team interview time, onboarding and training hours, reduced productivity during the transition, and administrative processing time[27].

gloss: Vacancy costs go beyond salary
verbatim: Vacancy costs extend well past the salary line item.

gloss: Recruitment marketing spend and background burnout/retention risk during a vacancy
verbatim: Money spent on job boards and other recruitment marketing platforms accumulates during the search, while team burnout and possible employee retention issues build in the background[28].

gloss: Hidden vacancy effects compound past tracked costs
verbatim: Lower productivity, missed deadlines, and decreased customer satisfaction round out the standard list of hidden vacancy effects, and these compound quickly, often exceeding the direct vacancy costs organizations actually track[28].

gloss: Hidden costs vary by industry/role (engineering, manufacturing, construction)

gloss: FAQ answering what cost per hire is, how to calculate it, and what the average 2026 CPH figures are by role level.
verbatim:
What is cost per hire?
Cost per hire (CPH) is the standardised talent acquisition metric measuring the total investment required to source, attract, assess, and onboard a new employee. The authoritative SHRM/ANSI formula is: CPH = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) / Total Number of Hires. Per SHRM 2026 Talent Access Benchmarking Report, average US CPH is approximately $4,700-$4,800 for non-executive roles and $28,329-$35,879 for executive hires.
How do you calculate cost per hire?
Use the SHRM/ANSI formula: CPH = (Internal Costs + External Costs) / Total Hires. Internal costs include recruiter salaries and overhead, hiring manager and interviewer time, HR administrative time, recruiting technology (ATS, sourcing tools), internal referral bonuses, and recruiting events. External costs include job board postings, recruitment advertising, agency or retained search fees, background checks and assessments, sign-on bonuses, relocation, and candidate travel. Divide all recruiting costs in a period by all hires made in that same period.
What’s the average cost per hire in 2026?
Per SHRM 2026 Talent Access Benchmarking Report: approximately $4,700-$4,800 for non-executive roles (US average). Executive roles average $28,329-$35,879 (up 21% from 2022). Significant variation by role: entry-level $1,500-$3,500; mid-level professional $3,500-$8,000; engineering $6,000-$23,000; senior management $10,000-$30,000; retained executive search $50,000-$250,000. Technology and financial services above average; retail and hospitality below average.
What costs are missing from the SHRM cost per hire formula?
The SHRM/ANSI formula does not include vacancy cost (productivity loss while a role sits empty), which is often larger than the recruiting investment. Per industry research: standard professional roles lose ~$500/day; revenue-generating sales roles lose $7,000-$10,000/month. With median 2026 US time-to-fill at 63.5 days, vacancy cost typically adds $22,000+ to the SHRM CPH for standard roles. Also excluded: ramp cost (new hires below full productivity for 3-12 months) and quality risk.
How do you reduce cost per hire?
Invest in employee referrals (consistently lowest CPH and highest quality), build internal sourcing capability (reduce agency dependence), optimise candidate experience (lower drop-off improves yield), use AI tools (mature implementations cut CPH 30%+), reduce time-to-fill (compounds savings via vacancy cost), track source-of-hire ROI rigorously, audit agency relationships, and build talent pools (pre-engaged candidates reduce future CPH dramatically).
Is a lower cost per hire always better?
No. If low-CPH hires leave quickly or underperform, the true hiring cost is much higher. CPH should be tracked alongside quality-of-hire, time-to-fill, candidate experience, source-of-hire effectiveness, and 90-day / 1-year retention. Quality-adjusted CPH, the cost per successful, retained, and productive hire, is the metric that matters for business outcomes.

gloss: Defines TA ROI as value returned vs. cost to run recruiting, and illustrates with two same-cost hires whose outcomes differ wildly.
verbatim:
Talent acquisition ROI, or TA ROI, is a measure of how much value your hiring process returns compared to what it costs to run. It treats recruiting as an investment, not overhead. The return on investment side includes faster time to productivity, lower turnover, and stronger on-the-job performance. The cost side includes recruiter salaries, advertising, assessment tools, and agency spend.

Think of two hires that each cost $5,000 to recruit. One ramps in a month, hits target, and stays three years. The other takes a quarter to get going and leaves within the year. Same cost on paper. Wildly different ROI. That gap is the whole reason this metric exists: it forces you to look past the invoice and at what the hire did once they walked in.
heading: What is talent acquisition ROI?

gloss: Gives the ROI formula (value gained minus cost, divided by cost), explains the cost-per-hire side via the ANSI/SHRM standard, and notes value must be estimated with proxies.
verbatim:
The basic formula is the same one you would use for any investment:

 Talent acquisition ROI = (Value gained from the hire – Cost to hire) / Cost to hire, shown as a percentage 

The cost side is the easy part. Add internal recruiting costs and external ones over the same period, then divide by hires made. That is the ANSI/SHRM cost-per-hire standard , and it lands U.S. employers at about $4,700 a hire on average. SHRM also notes the fully loaded cost of a hire can reach three to four times the position’s salary once you count soft costs like manager time, so a $60,000 role can cost $180,000 or more to fill. Roughly 30% to 40% of that is hard cost; the other 60% is soft cost you rarely see on an invoice.

The value side is harder, and that is where most ROI math falls apart. You cannot put an exact dollar figure on every hire, so use proxies: revenue per employee for sales roles, output or tickets closed for operational roles, and retention for everyone. The point is not false precision. It is a consistent method you apply the same way every quarter, so the trend is honest even if the absolute number is an estimate.

gloss: Breaks total cost to hire into hard costs (30-40%, invoiced items) and soft costs (60%, recruiter/manager time and ramp-up), totaling ~$180,000 for a $60,000 role.
verbatim: The denominator in your ROI formula has two layers that SHRM separates clearly. Hard costs (30-40% of total) are the ones on invoices: job board spend, agency fees, assessment tools, and background checks. Soft costs (roughly 60%) are the ones that never appear on a vendor invoice: recruiter hours, hiring manager interview time, and the productivity ramp while a new hire gets up to speed. Add both layers and a $60,000 role costs roughly $180,000 to fill when you count everything.
heading: What goes into the total cost to hire?

gloss: Worked numeric example calculating ROI for a customer success hire (210% good-hire case vs. -45% if the hire leaves at six months).
verbatim:
Role: a mid-level customer success manager at a $70,000 annual salary. Hard recruiting costs run to $21,000 (30% of salary, per SHRM’s cost-per-hire benchmarks). Soft costs – hiring manager interview time, onboarding coordination, and the first 30 days of reduced productivity – add another $14,000. Total cost to hire: $35,000.

The role sat open for 38 days. SHRM’s 2022 Human Capital Benchmarking Report puts average time to fill at 42 days for professional roles, so 38 days is typical. At $70,000 per year, each unfilled working day costs roughly $269 in lost output (annual salary divided by 260 working days). Vacancy cost: $10,200. Total investment: $45,200.

In year one, the hire retains and expands an account portfolio worth $140,000 in revenue – a conservative two-times salary multiple for a customer success role. Talent acquisition ROI = ($140,000 – $45,200) / $45,200 = 210% . For every dollar spent recruiting this hire, the business returned $3.10.

Now run the bad-hire version. Same $45,200 cost to hire. Hire leaves at month six. Year-one value drops to $70,000 (half the output, half the year). You incur a replacement cost of $45,200 a second time. Total cost: $90,400. Net value: $70,000 – $90,400 = -$20,400. ROI: -45% . One early exit flips a 210% return into a loss. That is the arithmetic case for measuring quality of hire.

Quality of hire is the metric that actually moves return on investment, and it is the one teams find hardest to pin down. It blends three signals: first-year performance ratings, retention past probation, and hiring-manager satisfaction with the match. In LinkedIn’s 2025 Future of Recruiting report (a survey of more than 1,000 talent pros), 93% said accurately assessing a candidate’s skills is central to improving quality of hire, and 61% believe AI can help them measure it better.

This is the gap a skills assessment closes. When a candidate takes a role-based test before the first interview, you get a baseline score you can compare against their later performance. That turns quality of hire from a gut feeling into a number, which is the only way to improve quality of hire on purpose rather than by luck.

 Pro Tip: Score quality of hire on a 1-to-5 scale that combines a pre-hire assessment result, a 90-day manager rating, and one-year retention. One blended number per hire makes the metric easy to trend, and easy to defend when finance asks what recruiting returned.

Because hiring is one of the largest controllable costs in any people-heavy business, and most of it is invisible. The danger is not the obvious spend; it is the bad hire you have to replace. SHRM research puts the cost of replacing one employee at one-half to two times their annual salary. At a $70,000 average salary, that is a $35,000 to $140,000 replacement cost per departure – and that is before counting the productivity gap while the seat sits open.

Put those two numbers next to each other. A $4,700 cost per hire looks tiny against a replacement cost that can hit two times salary. So the team that obsesses over shaving $500 off cost per hire, while ignoring a quality problem that causes early exits, is optimizing the wrong end. That is the core argument for measuring ROI: it stops you from saving pennies on recruiting while burning dollars on turnover.

gloss: Explains how ATS/analytics cut cost and pre-hire assessments raise quality, with a concrete example of a software company compressing time to fill via coding assessments.
verbatim:
Technology lifts ROI in two places: it cuts the cost and time of screening, and it raises the quality of who gets through. An applicant tracking system and recruiting analytics handle the first. Pre-hire skills assessments handle the second, and the second is where the bigger ROI sits, because quality of hire is what protects you from replacement cost.

Here is a concrete version. A 500-person software company hiring 20 engineers a quarter sends a coding assessment before any recruiter screen. The shortlist arrives already scored, so the first human conversation happens with candidates who can actually do the work. SHRM benchmarks average time to fill at 42 days for professional roles. A screening loop that used to run six weeks compresses to about ten days, and the interviewers stop spending time on people who were never going to pass the technical bar. Lower cost per hire and higher quality of hire, from the same change.

The catch, and there is always a catch, is that an assessment is only as good as its fit to the role. A generic test bolted onto a specialized job adds noise, not signal. Match the test to the actual work, and pair it with assessment data you actually review , or you are just adding a step.

verbatim:
Start with yourself, not the industry. Your own quarter-over-quarter trend is the most honest benchmark you have, because it controls for your roles, your market, and your pay bands. Pull three or four quarters of cost per hire, time to fill, quality of hire, and retention, and look at the direction of travel before you compare to anyone else.

Then bring in external numbers carefully. Industry averages like the $4,700 cost per hire are useful context, but they hide huge variation. A senior engineering hire in a tight market and a high-volume support hire are not the same line item, and an average blends them into a figure that fits neither. Use benchmarks to ask questions (why is our cost double the average for this role?), not to set targets you then game.

 Key Takeaway: ROI is a trend, not a trophy. One clean quarter proves nothing. The teams that improve hiring are the ones that read cost, speed, quality, and retention together, every quarter, and act on the one metric that is dragging the rest.

gloss: Describes the 'Testlify ROI Scorecard' quarterly loop: baseline, score quality pre-interview, connect the KPIs, and act on the weakest metric.
verbatim:
The answer is a consistent quarterly review loop. We call ours the Testlify ROI Scorecard. Four steps, run every quarter, it keeps the focus on the metric that matters instead of the one that is easiest to count.

- Baseline. Record cost per hire, time to fill, quality of hire, and retention for the last full quarter. This is your starting line. 
- Score quality before the interview. Run a role-based skills assessment up front, so every candidate gets a comparable quality score, not a resume guess. 
- Connect the numbers. Track each KPI together. If cost drops but quality or retention drops with it, the saving is not real. 
- Act on the weakest link. Fix the one metric dragging ROI down, then re-baseline next quarter. Repeat. 

None of this needs a data-science team. It needs a consistent method and a quality signal you trust. For more on the analytics side, our guide to analytics for smarter hiring goes deeper on the reporting setup.

verbatim:
What is a good ROI for talent acquisition? 

There is no single magic number, because it depends on the role and industry. A practical target is a recruiting spend that returns several times its cost through faster productive hiring, lower turnover, and stronger performance. Track the trend in your own cost per hire and quality of hire over time, then compare each new quarter against your own baseline rather than a generic benchmark.

 How do you calculate cost per hire? 

Add your internal recruiting costs (recruiter salaries, referral payouts) and external costs (job ads, agency fees, assessment tools) over a set period, then divide by the number of hires in that same period. This is the ANSI/SHRM standard formula , and SHRM put the U.S. average at nearly $4,700 per hire.

 What is the difference between time to fill and time to hire? 

Time to fill counts the days from when a job opens to when an offer is accepted, so it measures pipeline and process speed. Time to hire counts the days from when a candidate enters your pipeline to when they accept, so it measures how fast you move a single person through. Track both: one tells you about demand, the other about your funnel.

 How do you measure quality of hire? 

Quality of hire blends a few signals: first-year job performance ratings, new-hire retention past the probation period, and hiring-manager satisfaction with the match. A skills assessment taken before the first interview gives you a baseline score to compare against later performance, which is why 93% of talent pros told LinkedIn that accurately assessing skills is central to improving quality of hire.

 Which talent acquisition metric matters most? 

Quality of hire. Speed and cost are easy to count, but a cheap, fast hire who leaves in six months destroys ROI. SHRM research puts the cost of replacing one employee at one-half to two times their annual salary, so the metric that protects you from a bad hire is the one worth defending in a budget review.

What is recruitment analytics?

Plan for a phased build: quick wins from funnel data first, predictive capability from assessment linkage over time.
Why is recruitment analytics data siloed or incomplete at most companies?
Because recruiting data is generated by multiple systems that were not designed to communicate with each other – an ATS, a sourcing platform, an assessment tool, an HRIS, and sometimes a CRM. What is the difference between an ATS and a recruitment marketing tool?
An ATS manages candidates after they apply — tracking stages, storing resumes, and managing communications. Recruitment marketing tools work before the application: they attract candidates through job distribution, employer branding, and nurture campaigns. Most enterprise stacks use both together as complementary layers.
How much should an enterprise HR team budget for recruitment marketing tools?
Entry-level platforms (Manatal, TalentLyft, Teamtailor) run $100-$300/month for small teams. Mid-market platforms (Workable, Jobvite) typically range from $25,000-$75,000/year. Enterprise platforms (Phenom, Beamery, iCIMS) are custom-priced, often $100,000-$500,000/year depending on hiring volume.

No. They reduce administrative time — sourcing, screening, scheduling — so recruiters spend more time on relationship-building and assessment conversations. How do I measure ROI from recruitment marketing tools?
Four metrics matter: source-to-hire conversion rate (which channels produce hires), cost-per-hire by source, time-to-fill by role type, and quality-of-hire at 90 days (performance and retention rate). If your tools cannot report on at least two of these four metrics, upgrade the analytics layer before adding more sourcing spend.

gloss: Outlines Testlify's 5-Signal Hiring Model, a five-step process for building a data-driven recruitment pipeline from defining skill standards through tracking post-hire performance.
verbatim:
Building a data-driven recruitment process requires five connected steps: defining a measurable skills standard before the role opens, assessing candidates at the top of the funnel before any call, tracking conversion data at every stage, logging cost and time by source, and connecting post-hire performance back to the pre-hire scores that predicted it.
Testlify’s 5-Signal Hiring Model breaks that process into stages where data either informs the next action or flags a gap to address:
Signal 1: Define the skills standard before opening the role. Decide which two or three skills actually predict success in this position. Set the passing benchmark before reviewing a single application, so the standard cannot shift based on who applies.
Signal 2: Assess the full pool before the first call. Score every applicant on the defined skills using a standardized test. This narrows the shortlist to candidates who can already do the work, so interview time goes to judgment and fit rather than basic qualification.
Signal 3: Track funnel conversion at every stage. Record how many candidates move from application to assessment, assessment to interview, interview to offer, and offer to acceptance. A stage with high drop-off has either a process problem or a sourcing problem; the data shows which.
Signal 4: Record cost and time data by source and role. Not all sourcing channels produce equivalent-quality hires. Tracking cost-per-qualified-candidate, not just cost-per-hire, reveals which channels are actually worth the budget allocation.
Signal 5: Connect post-hire performance back to pre-hire scores. At the 90-day and 12-month review, compare employee performance ratings to their original assessment scores. This loop validates the assessment design and shows where the model needs recalibration.
This is the core of how analytics sharpens hiring decisions: the data is only useful when it changes what the team does next.

gloss: Defines Time to Fill, gives SHRM benchmark (~44 days average, varying by industry), and quantifies the cost of a vacant role (~1/3 of annual salary per month).
verbatim:
Time to Fill is the number of calendar days between the date a job requisition is officially opened and the date a candidate accepts an offer. It is one of the most widely tracked recruitment metrics and, when used correctly, one of the most powerful early warning signals in your hiring system.
What the data says
According to SHRM’s Talent Acquisition Benchmarking Report, the average Time to Fill across all industries in the United States is approximately 44 days. But breaking that number down by context tells a much more useful story:
- Technology and engineering roles average 60 to 80 days due to talent scarcity and multi-stage interview processes
- Healthcare and clinical roles average 49 days, with specialist positions running significantly longer
- Retail and hospitality roles should ideally close in under 21 days, given high volume and urgency
- Financial services roles average around 40 days, though senior and compliance-heavy roles take longer
Why it matters beyond the numbers
Every open role carries a cost that never shows up in your recruitment budget. Research from the Society for Human Resource Management estimates that a vacant position costs organizations an average of one-third of that role’s annual salary per month in lost productivity, team strain, and missed deliverables.
For a position paying $90,000 per year, that is $30,000 sitting on the table every single month the seat is empty.
What slows time to fill down most often
- Internal approval bottlenecks before the role even goes live, which account for 20 to 30% of total fill time in most organizations
- Poorly written job descriptions that attract the wrong candidates and inflate screening time
- Interview panel scheduling conflicts that add days or weeks to each stage
- Lack of alignment between hiring managers and recruiters on the ideal candidate profile
How to track it effectively
Set job category benchmarks, not a single company-wide target. A 30-day Time to Fill is excellent for a customer service coordinator and concerning for a machine learning engineer.
Your ATS should be calculating this automatically, and alerts should trigger when specific roles breach category thresholds, prompting a proactive sourcing review rather than a reactive scramble.
heading: Time to fill

gloss: Defines Time to Hire, cites LinkedIn/Talent Board data on candidates dropping out of slow processes, and gives stage-by-stage benchmark targets (application-to-contact, interview-to-offer, etc.).
verbatim:
Time to hire measures the number of days from when a candidate first applies to when they accept an offer. Where Time to Fill looks at organizational efficiency, Time to Hire looks at the candidate’s experience of your process speed and reflects how competitive you are in real time.
The competitive reality in 2026
The talent market has fundamentally shifted the power dynamic in hiring. LinkedIn’s Global Talent Trends research consistently shows that top candidates are off the market within 10 days of beginning their job search.
Separately, a survey by the candidate experience platform Talent Board found that 60% of candidates have abandoned a job application midway through because the process was too long or too complex.
For employers, the implication is stark. A slow process is not just an inconvenience but a direct competitive disadvantage.
Key time to hire benchmarks by stage
- Application to first contact: Ideally, within 48 hours, with a hard ceiling of 5 business days
- First contact to interview: No more than 7 days, candidates interpret long gaps as disorganization
- Interview to offer: 3 to 5 business days for most roles, though technical assessments may extend this slightly
- Offer to acceptance: 48 to 72 hours in most cases, with senior roles allowing up to a week
What is actually slowing your time to hire
Most hiring leaders assume candidate availability is the primary driver of delays. Research suggests otherwise. The biggest contributors to the slow time to hire are:
- Interviewer feedback latency, with panels often taking 3 to 5 days to submit structured feedback after interviews
- Unclear decision-making authority, where multiple stakeholders need to approve each stage without a defined process
- Poorly calibrated technical assessments that are too long or too complex, causing candidate dropout
- Scheduling friction, particularly across time zones or with senior panel members whose calendars are heavily restricted
How to track time to hire effectively
Break Time to Hire down by stage rather than tracking only the total. A stage-level view tells you exactly where candidates are waiting and gives you specific, actionable targets for improvement. Implement 24-hour feedback submission requirements for all interviewers and track compliance as a separate metric within your TA operations dashboard.

gloss: Covers Quality of Hire as the most valuable but hardest-to-measure KPI, cites cost-of-bad-hire stats (30-200% of salary), and outlines a weighted composite scoring approach (performance rating, retention, etc.).
verbatim:
If there is one KPI that separates mature talent acquisition functions from reactive ones, it is Quality of Hire. It is the most strategically significant metric in recruitment and, by a wide margin, the hardest one to measure well.
Quality of Hire is a composite measure that evaluates how much real value a new hire delivers to the organization relative to expectations at the time of hire. It is not a single data point. It is a story told across multiple signals over time.
Why it matters more than any other metric
A LinkedIn survey of talent acquisition professionals found that Quality of Hire is considered the single most valuable KPI by 40% of respondents, outranking Time to Fill, Cost Per Hire, and every other metric. And yet fewer than a third of organizations have a consistent, documented method for measuring it.
The cost of ignoring it is high. Research from the U.S. Department of Labor estimates that a bad hire can cost up to 30% of the employee’s first year’s earnings.
SHRM puts that figure higher, suggesting the total cost, including lost productivity, management time, and recruitment can reach 50 to 60% of annual salary for mid-level roles and 200% or more for senior leadership positions.
How to build your Quality of Hire composite score
There is no universal formula, but the most effective models combine the following signals with weighted importance:
- Performance rating at 90 days and 6 months (suggested weight: 35 to 40%)
- 12-month retention, whether the employee is still with the organization at the one-year mark (suggested weight: 25 to 30%)
- Hiring manager satisfaction score collected via structured post-hire surveys at 30, 60, and 90 days (suggested weight: 15 to 20%)
- Speed to full productivity or ramp time compared to the role average (suggested weight: 10 to 15%)
- Peer and team lead cultural fit rating from a brief structured assessment (suggested weight: 5 to 10%)
How to track it effectively
The infrastructure for tracking Quality of Hire lives across your ATS, your HRIS, and your performance management system. That means tracking it well requires genuine cross-functional collaboration between Talent Acquisition, People Analytics, and line managers.
Automate post-hire survey triggers in your HRIS at 30, 60, and 90 days post start date. Make hiring manager participation non-negotiable by tying it to recruiter close-out processes. And most importantly, aggregate your Quality of Hire scores by source channel so you understand not just how well you are hiring overall, but which parts of your sourcing strategy are generating the most valuable hires.

gloss: Covers Source of Hire, explains why attribution data is usually unreliable (inconsistent labels, single-touch models, dark social), and shows referrals outperform other channels in hires and retention.
verbatim:
Source of Hire tracks which channel or touchpoint brought each successfully hired candidate into your pipeline. On the surface, it sounds straightforward. In practice, it is one of the most misunderstood and underutilized KPIs in recruitment analytics.
Why most source attribution data is broken
A 2024 survey by recruiting software company Jobvite found that nearly half of talent acquisition teams describe their source of hire data as “somewhat unreliable” or “unreliable.” The reasons are predictable:
- Recruiters use inconsistent source labels in their ATS, creating data that cannot be meaningfully aggregated
- Single-touch attribution models credit only the last channel a candidate interacted with before applying, ignoring the full journey
- Candidates themselves often cannot accurately recall where they first heard about a role, particularly if they were passively sourced
- Dark social channels, including direct referrals via text or private messaging, go entirely untracked
What clean source attribution actually reveals
When organizations do track Source of Hire accurately, the findings consistently challenge conventional wisdom about where recruiting budgets should go. Research from iCIMS and LinkedIn’s combined talent data suggests the following patterns hold true across most industries:
- Employee referrals produce 30 to 50% of all hires while consuming roughly 5 to 10% of total sourcing spend
- Referral hires have a first-year retention rate 45% higher than hires from job boards
- Direct sourcing through LinkedIn and professional outreach produces higher Quality of Hire scores than most inbound channels
- Job board spend, which consumes 30 to 40% of most external recruiting budgets, produces a disproportionately low share of high-quality, long-tenure hires
The multi-touch attribution advantage
The emerging standard in 2026 is multi-touch attribution, which credits all channels a candidate engaged with before applying, rather than just the last one. Practically, this means using UTM parameters on all digital sourcing links, integrating your careers site analytics with your ATS, and building a consistent tagging taxonomy that all recruiters follow without exception.
How to track the source of hire effectively
Run a quarterly source performance review that looks at three dimensions for each channel: volume of hires, average Quality of Hire score, and cost per hire from that channel. A channel that generates volume but scores low on quality and high on cost is actively costing you more than it appears to be delivering. That analysis alone will reshape most recruiting budgets.

gloss: Covers Cost Per Hire, breaks down internal vs external cost components, and gives SHRM/benchmark cost ranges by role seniority (entry-level to executive).
verbatim:
Cost Per Hire is the total investment required to successfully fill one open position. It is a KPI that most organizations track in some form, but very few track honestly. The gap between what teams think they spend on hiring and what they actually spend is almost always significant.
Breaking down the true cost of hire
Internal costs include:
- Hiring manager and interview panel time (often overlooked but frequently the largest single cost component)
- HR technology and ATS licensing fees
- Employee referral bonuses
- Internal onboarding and training overhead
External costs include:
- Job board advertising fees (LinkedIn, Indeed, niche boards)
- Recruitment agency or executive search fees, which typically range from 15 to 25% of the first year’s salary
- Background screening and pre-employment assessment tools
- Employer branding and careers site investment
- Relocation packages and signing bonuses were applicable
What the benchmarks say
SHRM’s most recent data puts the average Cost Per Hire in the United States at approximately $4,700, but this figure masks enormous variation by role level and function. More realistic breakdowns look like this:
- Entry-level and high-volume roles: $1,500 to $3,000 per hire
- Mid-level professional roles: $5,000 to $10,000 per hire
- Senior individual contributors and managers: $15,000 to $30,000 per hire
- Director level and above with executive search involvement: $30,000 to $100,000 or more
The most important cost per hire insight
Cost per hire only becomes a genuinely useful metric when it is read alongside Quality of Hire. A $2,000 hire who exits in six months or underperforms for two years is dramatically more expensive than a $15,000 hire who stays for five years and exceeds expectations.
Teams that optimize cost per hire in isolation consistently make this mistake, cutting corners on sourcing, assessment, and candidate experience to reduce spend, and then wondering why retention and performance outcomes suffer.
The right question to ask is not “how do we lower cost per hire?” It is “how do we optimize cost per hire relative to the quality and longevity of the hires we make?”

gloss: Covers Offer Acceptance Rate, gives benchmark tiers (90%+ healthy down to below 70% crisis), and attributes low acceptance to three root causes led by compensation misalignment.
verbatim:
Offer Acceptance Rate is the percentage of formal job offers that candidates accept. It is the final checkpoint in your hiring funnel, and its performance is a direct report card on how well you understand your candidates, your market, and your own employer brand.
How to calculate the offer acceptance rate
What the benchmarks tell you
- 90% or above: Healthy and competitive. Your compensation, EVP, and candidate experience are aligned with market expectations.
- 80 to 89%: Acceptable but worth investigating by role type and source. There may be pockets of misalignment that aggregated data is masking.
- 70 to 79%: A meaningful problem. One in four candidates you invest in reaching the offer stage is choosing someone else. Immediate diagnosis is warranted.
- Below 70%: A crisis state. This level indicates systemic misalignment between what you are offering and what the market expects, and it is costing you enormous amounts of wasted hiring investment.
The three root causes of low offer acceptance rates
Nearly every decline in the Offer Acceptance Rate traces back to one of three sources:
Compensation misalignment
Compensation misalignment is the most common and most preventable cause. A survey by Mercer found that 68% of candidates who declined job offers cited total compensation as the primary reason.
The fix is simple: conduct formal salary benchmarking at the job description stage, not at the offer stage.
Candidate experience breakdown
Candidate experience breakdown occurs when the interview process itself erodes a candidate’s enthusiasm for the role. Slow feedback, disorganized logistics, inconsistent messaging from interviewers, and a lack of genuine engagement all signal to a candidate that the organization’s culture may not match its pitch.
A weak Employee Value Proposition (EVP)
A weak Employee Value Proposition (EVP) is the hardest to fix but the most important to address. In 2026, candidates research employers the way consumers research products. Glassdoor data shows that 86% of job seekers read company reviews before deciding whether to apply, and that number only rises as candidates progress through an interview process.
If your EVP is unclear, inconsistent, or not reflected in how your interviewers present the role, candidates will notice.
How to track offer acceptance rates effectively
Beyond the rate itself, build a structured decline tracking process. Every declined offer should be followed by a brief exit survey or recruiter conversation that captures the primary reason for declining.
Categorize decline reasons consistently across: compensation, competing offer, role fit concerns, process experience, location or flexibility, and EVP or culture. Track the distribution of those categories quarterly and look for trends. This data is arguably the most direct competitive intelligence a talent acquisition team can collect.

gloss: Covers Candidate Experience Score, explains the NPS-style measurement method (promoters/passives/detractors) and why it's a business-wide metric, not just HR's.
verbatim:
Candidate Experience Score quantifies how candidates perceive and feel about your recruitment process from the first touchpoint to final outcome. It is, without question, the most underinvested KPI in most organizations’ talent acquisition dashboards, and in 2026, it carries consequences that extend well beyond the HR function.
How to measure it
The most widely adopted and reliable approach is a candidate Net Promoter Score, adapted from the customer experience methodology. Ask every candidate who moves through your process, regardless of outcome, the following question:
“On a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend applying to this company to a friend or colleague?”
Responses are segmented as follows:
- 9 to 10: Promoters, candidates who had a positive experience and are likely to recommend your company to others
- 7 to 8: Passives, candidates who had a neutral experience and are unlikely to either advocate or discourage others
- 0 to 6: Detractors, candidates who had a negative experience and may actively warn others against applying
Supplement the overall score with stage-specific pulse surveys after key milestones: application acknowledgment, post-interview, and post-offer. Stage-level data tells you exactly which parts of your process are creating friction.
Why this is a business metric, not just an HR metric
The business case for Candidate Experience is compelling and frequently underestimated:
- According to IBM’s Smarter Workforce Institute, candidates who have a positive experience are 38% more likely to accept a job offer
- The Talent Board’s annual Candidate Experience Research Report found that candidates who have a negative experience are twice as likely to sever their relationship with that company as a consumer
- Glassdoor research shows that organizations with strong candidate experience scores receive 50% more qualified applicants, reducing sourcing costs and improving the overall talent pool quality
- In industries where the candidate pool and customer base overlap, such as retail, hospitality, financial services, and healthcare, a poor hiring experience can directly impact revenue
Common candidate experience failures and their fixes
Silence after application submission: This is the number one driver of negative candidate sentiment. Implement automated acknowledgment messages within 24 hours of every application received, regardless of whether the candidate progresses.
Long gaps between interview stages: Long gaps between interview stages without proactive communication create anxiety and signal disorganization. Assign a dedicated point of contact for every candidate in process and set a standard that no candidate should go more than 5 business days without hearing from your team.
Poor rejection communication: Research has found that 70% of candidates who had a negative experience cited poor or nonexistent rejection communication as a primary reason. A thoughtful, timely rejection message costs nothing and preserves both the candidate’s goodwill and your employer brand.
Inconsistent interviewer behavior: When you have some interviewers who are prepared and communicative, while others are distracted, late, or dismissive, it creates unpredictable experiences that are difficult to manage at scale.
Interviewer training and structured interview scorecards are the standard fix, and they improve both candidate experience and Quality of Hire simultaneously.
How to track candidate experience score
Automate survey delivery through your ATS or CRM at each stage of the candidate journey. Review Candidate NPS monthly, segment by role type, hiring manager, and interview stage. Most importantly, act on the feedback visibly and communicate what has changed. Candidates and employees both notice when their input leads to tangible improvement, and that response in itself becomes a positive signal about your organizational culture.

The cost-per-hire calculator uses the following formula to calculate the total hiring costs:
Cost-per-hire (CPH)= (External costs) + (Internal costs) / Total number of hires in a period

gloss: FAQ answers covering what counts as good ROI (30-70%), how to measure return for non-revenue roles, EOR vs contractor cost-effectiveness, and whether pay transparency improves offer acceptance.
verbatim:
What does a 70% ROI mean?
A 70% recruitment ROI means your hiring return is 70% higher than what you spent. So if you invested $100, you got the $100 back and about $70 more in value. It usually signals the process is working well and not wasting time or cost.
Is a 30% ROI good?
Yes, 30% is generally a healthy ROI. It means hiring is adding more value than it costs. Whether it’s “great” depends on the role type, hiring market, and how you calculate returns, but it’s a positive sign.
How do you calculate the “Return” for non-revenue roles?
For non-revenue roles, return is measured through business impact, not sales. Use proxies like time saved, faster delivery, fewer errors, reduced overtime, lower operating cost, and retention. If you hire in lower-cost regions, you can also include the savings compared to your baseline market.
Is it more cost-effective to use an EOR or hire international contractors?
Contractors can look cheaper upfront, but the risk is misclassification and compliance issues. An EOR costs more in service fees, but they handle local employment compliance, payroll, and taxes. In many cases, it comes down to how long you need the role and how much risk you can take.
Does pay transparency in job ads improve offer acceptance?
In most cases, yes. When candidates know the pay range early, you avoid late-stage surprises and drop-offs. It also attracts people who are a better fit from the start, which improves conversions and reduces wasted interview time.

There’s a pattern in technical hiring that doesn’t get talked about enough. A company opens a developer role, writes a job description, runs candidates through assessments, picks the best performer, extends an offer, and then discovers the budget doesn’t match the market rate for that skill level.
